card werk-onelock-hardlink  [decided]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
A reader of the server lock sees a whole lock or none, never a half-written one
why: A starting server reads the lock to find the pid of the holder. If it reads the lock while another process writes it, it finds no pid. Then it takes a live lock for a stale one, and two servers share one directory.

The lock holds the pid and the port of the server (see #werk-onelock). The lock changes at two moments: a start takes it, and the holder records its port after the listen succeeds. A second start can read the lock at either moment.

To avoid a half-written read, every change to the lock is complete before any reader can see it:

- When a start takes the lock, the lock appears whole, or not at all. When two starts take it at the same moment, only one succeeds.
- When the holder records its port, a reader sees the old lock or the new lock, never a mix and never an empty file.

Example:

- Server A holds the lock: pid 100, no port yet.
- The listen of A succeeds on port 4211.
- Start B reads the lock at the same moment.

1. A writes the new lock, pid 100 and port 4211, out of sight of readers.
2. A puts the new lock in place in one step.
3. B reads the lock. It sees pid 100 with no port, or pid 100 with port 4211.
4. Pid 100 is alive in both cases. B waits, then refuses to start.
5. B never sees an empty lock, so B never removes the lock of A as stale.

```
  A: lock {pid 100, no port}     B: reads lock
          |                               |
  1 A writes {pid 100, port 4211} aside   |
          |                               |
  2 A swaps it in, one step  ---------  3 B sees {100, no port}
          |                               or {100, 4211}
          v                               |
  A: lock {pid 100, port 4211}   4 pid 100 alive -> B waits, refuses

  never:  B sees {}  ->  "stale"  ->  two servers
```

One werk server per .werk directory
why: Two servers share the session id and the transcript. It looks like the agent losing its memory at random.

On 2026-09-04 test servers ran against the live .werk directory while another server was serving it. They overwrote the stored session id with throwaway test conversations and interleaved their transcripts into the chat transcript. The pane showed "Session 1dcacf3e could not be resumed" and synthetic errors from tests the user never ran.

It was first read as a transient fault that could not be reproduced. That was wrong. The cause was two servers sharing one directory.

The server takes a lock file in .werk, holding the pid and the port. A second server checks whether that pid is alive and refuses:

    werk: another werk is already serving this repository on port 4211 (pid 89491).
    werk: stop it first, or run in a different directory. One server per .werk.

A stale lock from a killed process is ignored, because the pid check fails. The lock is released on exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Set WERK_LOG to point at another directory to run a second instance on purpose. Tests run that way.

A werk server owns live state in the `.werk` directory, and that state has room for only one writer. The answer is on the parent card, #werk-onelock.

1. **Session id.** The server stores one Claude Code session id. A restart uses it to resume the chat (#werk-resume). A second server overwrites it with its own id, so the pane resumes the wrong conversation.
2. **Transcript.** Both servers append to the same chat transcript, so their lines mix together.
3. **What the user sees.** The agent seems to lose its memory at random. One example error is "Session 1dcacf3e could not be resumed".

This happened on 2026-09-04. Test servers ran against the live `.werk` directory while the real server was still serving it. At first it looked like a fault nobody could reproduce. The real cause was two servers on one directory.

The lock is the guard against this. A second server reads the pid in the lock, sees that the process is alive, and refuses to start. The card you have open closes one gap in that guard. If the second server reads a half-written lock, it finds no pid and treats the lock as stale. Then both servers run.

An agent session started them by mistake. On 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-04, the agent tested the chat pane end to end. Several cards were verified that night, for example the permission checks on #werk-approve. For each test, the agent started a real `werk serve`. Those servers used the default `.werk` directory of the repository. That was the same directory your live server was serving.

Nothing prevented this:

1. `serve` had no lock, so any number of servers could start on one directory.
2. The tests did not set `WERK_LOG` to a separate directory.

The test servers wrote throwaway session ids into `.werk/session`. They also appended their turns to the chat transcript. Your pane then failed to resume, and it showed errors from tests you never ran. The first diagnosis was "a transient fault that we cannot reproduce". That diagnosis was wrong.

The fix had two parts. Tests now run with `WERK_LOG` pointed at a separate directory, and `serve` takes the lock. Source: the first version of #werk-onelock in the log, 2026-09-03 23:00 UTC.

Only one start at a time may remove a stale lock
why: A start reads the lock, sees a dead holder, and then removes the lock. These are two steps. A second start that read the same stale lock can remove a fresh lock that a third start took in between, and then two servers share one log.

A stale lock is a lock whose holder process is dead (see #werk-onelock). The lock itself is taken in one step that fails when a lock exists (see #werk-onelock-hardlink). The removal of a stale lock is not one step, so it needs its own protection.

To avoid the race, a start takes a second, short-lived lock, the guard, before it removes a stale lock. The guard is taken in the same one-step way as the lock and holds the pid of its holder. Under the guard, the start reads the lock again. It removes the lock only if the lock still names a dead process. Then it drops the guard and tries to take the lock again. A start that finds the guard taken waits one poll interval and tries again.

A guard whose holder is dead is removed like a stale lock. That removal has no guard of its own. It goes wrong only if a start dies inside the short removal step and two other starts race over its guard.

Example:

card werk-onelock-lockfile  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The lock is .werk/server.lock beside the log, taken with an exclusive create
why: An exclusive create (O_EXCL) makes two starts race safely: only one of them creates the file.

The lock file sits in the directory of the log, so WERK_LOG moves the lock with the log. It holds {pid, port} as JSON. The port is null until the listen succeeds, then the file is rewritten with it. A holder whose pid is dead is a stale lock: the start removes it and tries again. A live holder: the start prints 'werk: waiting for pid N to let go of the lock', polls every 100 ms for 5 s, then refuses with the #werk-onelock message. The lock is removed on exit, SIGINT and SIGTERM, and only when it still holds this pid.

node src/cli.ts say werk-onelock-hardlink "Checked against the current server code. A start that reads an empty or half-written lock fails to parse it and exits, so it refuses to start. That failure is safe, not the shared-directory case in the why. The open gap is different: the check for a lock and the write of the lock are two steps, so two starts in the same moment can both pass. The exclusive create on #werk-onelock-lockfile closes that gap."
noted on werk-onelock-hardlink

Do not accept it as written. Its why describes a failure that the current code does not have.

I checked the lock code in the server:

1. **Half-written read.** Suppose start B reads an empty or partial lock. B cannot parse it, so B crashes and does not start. That outcome is safe. B never takes a live lock for a stale one, so the why on this card is wrong for the current code.
2. **The real gap.** The server first checks for a lock and then writes its own lock. These are two separate steps. Two starts in the same moment can both find no lock and both start. An exclusive create closes this gap: the file write fails when the file already exists. #werk-onelock-lockfile proposes this fix.
3. **How likely it is.** The gap needs two `serve` starts within a few milliseconds of each other. The 2026-09-04 incident had a different cause: there was no lock at all. The current lock already prevents that.

My recommendation:

1. Use the exclusive create from #werk-onelock-lockfile. The change is about one line. That card needs new wording first: it names `server.lock`, but the code uses `serve.lock`.
2. Defer or discard #werk-onelock-hardlink and #werk-onelock-reap-guard. Both add work for a race that a person must start by hand within milliseconds.

I put the code check as a note on the card.

  --body 'The lock is a file in the same directory as the log, so a log in another directory has its own lock. It holds the pid and the port of the holder (see #werk-onelock).

To avoid two starts that both find no lock, a start creates the lock file in one step that fails when the file exists. Exactly one start succeeds. A start whose create fails reads the lock. A dead pid means a stale lock: the start removes it and creates again. A live pid means a running server: the start polls until that server exits, and refuses at the end of the wait. A lock that does not parse counts as held during the wait, because its holder can be between the create and the write. If it still does not parse at the end of the wait, it counts as stale, because its holder died between the two.

The removal of a stale lock has no guard. Two starts that read the same stale lock in the same moment can both run. That needs two starts within milliseconds of each other right after a crash, and the lock accepts that risk.

Example:

- No server runs. Starts B and C begin at the same moment.
- Later, B is killed with no clean exit. Start D begins.

1. B creates the lock. The create succeeds. B runs.
2. C creates the lock. The create fails, because the file exists.
3. C reads the lock. It is empty, because B has not written yet. C waits and reads again.
4. C reads pid B. B is alive. C polls until the wait ends, then refuses.
5. B is killed. The lock stays and still names pid B.
6. D creates the lock. The create fails. D reads pid B, and B is dead.
7. D removes the stale lock, creates it again, and runs.

```
  B: create ──> ok ──────────────> lock {pid B}   B runs
  C: create ──> exists
     read ──> {} (not parsed) ──> wait, read again
     read ──> {pid B}, B alive ──> poll ... refuse

  B killed: lock {pid B} remains, B dead
  D: create ──> exists ──> read {pid B}, dead ──> remove ──> create ──> ok   D runs

  {}      = empty lock, not parsed yet
  {pid B} = lock that names the pid of B
```'

card werk-onelock-take  [decided]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
why: If a start first checks for a lock and then writes one, two starts at the same moment can both find no lock and both run. One create step that fails when the file already exists lets only one of them win. The loser then reads the lock to decide whether to wait or to take over a stale one.
To avoid two starts that both find no lock, a start creates the lock file in one step that fails when the file exists. Exactly one start succeeds. A start whose create fails reads the lock. A dead pid means a stale lock: the start removes it and creates again. A live pid means a running server: the start polls until that server exits, and refuses at the end of the wait. A lock that does not parse counts as held during the wait, because its holder can be between the create and the write. If it still does not parse at the end of the wait, it counts as stale, because its holder died between the two.
The removal of a stale lock has no guard. Two starts that read the same stale lock in the same moment can both run. That needs two starts within milliseconds of each other right after a crash, and the lock accepts that risk.
7. D removes the stale lock, creates it again, and runs.

#werk-onelock-take is proposed and decided. It waits for your ✓. It replaces four ghosts with one card:

1. **Take the lock.** A start creates the lock in one step. The step fails when the lock file already exists. Only one of two concurrent starts wins.
2. **Unreadable lock.** A lock that does not parse counts as held during the wait. If it is still unreadable at the end of the wait, it counts as stale. A start no longer crashes on it.
3. **Stale removal has no guard.** The card accepts this risk. Its kill criterion: two servers on one directory, seen even once.
